reason: The text does not present the people's complaint as sinful or inappropriate. When the elders of Israel ask 'Why has the Lord defeated us today before the Philistines?' (וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ זִקְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לָ֣מָּה נְגָפָ֧נוּ יְהוָ֛ה הַיּ֖וֹם לִפְנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים), the narrative records this question without moral condemnation. The actual theological focus of the passage is on God's judgment of Eli's corrupt household, the failure of Eli's priestly leadership, and the rise of Samuel as God's faithful prophet. The Israelites' defeat is not presented as punishment for complaining, but as consequence of broader spiritual corruption. The narrative does not extract a moral teaching against people complaining to leaders; rather, it implicitly critiques failed leadership itself.
